chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Diagnosed malformed utility model request in memory recall pipeline Got it. The error is clear — enabling memory_recall_query_prep: true made _50_recall_memories.py start calling self.agent.call_utility_model() at line 83 to have GLM-4.7 Flash generate an optimized search query before the vector DB lookup. That call is throwing a BadRequestError from litellm, which means the request is reaching LM Studio but being rejected. The looping happens because the memory recall fires every message (interval: 1), fails, the agent retries or proceeds with a broken state, and the cycle repeats. Most likely causes, in order of probability: The utility model prompt for keyword extraction is too long or malformed for GLM-4.7 Flash. Agent-zero uses memory.keyword_extraction.sys.md and memory.keyword_extraction.msg.md as the prompt templates for query prep. If those templates produce a payload that exceeds GLM-4.7's context or contains formatting it chokes on, you get exactly this error. The utility model slot in settings isn't pointing at the right model string. LM Studio sometimes needs the exact model identifier — if there's a mismatch between what litellm sends and what LM Studio expects, it returns a 400.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Empty or malformed message content. If the conversation history is empty on the first turn, the keyword extraction prompt might produce an empty messages array or null content field, which litellm rejects. Immediate fix — disable query prep, keep everything else: bash # Edit your settings to turn off just the failing feature # Change memory_recall_query_prep back to false # Keep interval at 1 and everything else enabled Change memory_recall_query_prep to false and memory_recall_post_filter to false in your settings override. Both of those call the utility model. The memory system will still work — it just uses raw message text for the vector search instead of an AI-refined query. Given that your FAISS embeddings are semantic similarity anyway, the quality difference is marginal. If you want to debug rather than bypass: # Check what prompt is being assembled cat /a0/prompts/memory.keyword_extraction.sys.md cat /a0/prompts/memory.keyword_extraction.msg.md # Check the exact line that fails sed -n '75,95p' /a0/python/extensions/message_loop_prompts_after/_50_recall_memories.py

chunks.text: Immediate fix: bash # In your settings override, disable both utility model calls in memory: # memory_recall_query_prep: false # memory_recall_post_filter: false # Keep everything else you changed This keeps memory recall active at interval 1, still searches FAISS every message, but uses the raw conversation text as the search query instead of asking the utility model to refine it. chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Now the strategic question: GPT-OSS-20B vs Qwen3-14B for your agent stack. Short answer: GPT-OSS-20B is worth testing but not as a wholesale replacement. Here's why. What GPT-OSS-20B brings that Qwen3 doesn't: The 20B model has 21B total parameters but only 3.6B active per token thanks to MoE, and it fits within 16GB of memory. GitHub That's extremely efficient on your RTX 3090's 24GB. It was explicitly designed for agentic workflows with native function calling, web browsing, Python code execution, and Structured Outputs. OpenAI OpenAI benchmarks show it matches or exceeds o3-mini on competition coding, general problem solving, and tool calling, and it even outperforms o4-mini on health-related queries and competition math. The native tool calling is the big differentiator. Qwen3-14B does tool calling, but it wasn't architecturally optimized for it the way GPT-OSS was. And tool calling reliability is exactly where your agent loops break. What makes this complicated: GPT-OSS was trained using OpenAI's "harmony response format" and should only be used with this format — otherwise it won't work correctly.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: LM Studio LM Studio handles this by utilizing the Harmony library to construct inputs and exposing a Chat Completions-compatible API Openai , so from litellm's perspective it looks like a standard OpenAI endpoint. But here's the catch — litellm has a known open issue where it doesn't properly support reasoning content from GPT-OSS models served in Harmony format , specifically around chain-of-thought tokens. Since agent-zero routes everything through litellm, you could hit edge cases where the response parsing breaks. Direct benchmark comparisons show that while GPT-OSS-20B generally leads in agentic and reasoning tasks, Qwen3-14B is more efficient, faster, and better suited for multilingual or edge deployments. Dasroot Qwen3 often provides better alignment and reasoning depth on complex use cases, while GPT-OSS is more memory efficient. Medium And the hallucination rate matters for your pipeline — GPT-OSS has notably higher hallucination rates compared to proprietary models, with SimpleQA accuracy around 0.168 versus roughly 0.234 for o4-mini.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Local AI Zone For an agent that's making file system decisions and running commands, hallucinated paths and tool parameters are exactly the failure mode you've been fighting. My actual recommendation for your setup: Don't frame this as "switch to GPT-OSS" — frame it as "add GPT-OSS-20B to the model roster." Your prosthetics architecture is model-agnostic by design. The BST doesn't care what model sits below it. That's the whole point of deterministic preprocessing. The optimal configuration for your RTX 3090 would be to test GPT-OSS-20B as the utility model replacing GLM-4.7 Flash. Its MoE architecture means only 3.6B parameters are active per token, so it's fast for the structured subtasks the utility model handles (keyword extraction, memory filtering, summarization). Its native tool calling and structured output capability could actually reduce the need for some of the prosthetics on the utility side. Keep Qwen3-14B (or upgrade to Qwen3-30B if VRAM allows with model swapping) as supervisor. The BST, the prompt patches, and all the scaffolding you've built are tuned for Qwen's behavioral patterns. Switching the supervisor means re-tuning confidence thresholds, trigger words, and preamble templates across all 18 intent domains.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: As for whether to build prosthetics that are model-agnostic across both families — yes, absolutely. That's the right engineering direction. The BST taxonomy should have a model_hints field per domain that adjusts preamble language based on which model family is active. GPT-OSS responds better to structured function-calling syntax; Qwen responds better to imperative natural language. One taxonomy, two rendering paths. Re: should you switch frameworks entirely — no. Agent-zero's architecture is what you know, you've already mapped its internals, and the prosthetics you've built are specific to its extension hooks. The value of GPT-OSS isn't that it needs a different framework — it's that it might need fewer prosthetics for certain tasks because tool calling is baked into its training objective rather than bolted on via prompt engineering.

chunks.text: Evaluated optimal utility model constraints for agentic architecture Good — that bash output confirms the utility model is a completely separate config slot. Let me look at what's optimal for that role right now. Evaluated MoE models and VRAM constraints for optimal utility model selection Good question. The utility model slot has very different requirements from the supervisor — it needs to be fast, reliable at structured output, and small enough to coexist with Qwen3-14B in your 24GB VRAM budget. Let me break down the actual candidates. Your VRAM budget reality: Qwen3-14B at Q4_K_M is roughly 10GB loaded. That leaves you ~12-13GB for the utility model plus KV cache overhead. If LM Studio is swapping models (loading one, unloading the other), you have the full 24GB — but that introduces latency every time agent-zero calls the utility model, which happens frequently (memory recall, keyword extraction, post-filtering). The three models worth testing, ranked by fit for your specific utility slot:

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: 1. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 — This is the one I'd try first. It's a Mixture-of-Experts model with 30B total parameters but only 3B active per token, and it was specifically optimized for instruction following, tool usage, and complex reasoning tasks including multi-step code reasoning and tool-augmented workflows. KDnuggets The 3B active parameter count means inference is fast — comparable to running a 3B dense model — but you get the knowledge depth of a 30B model because the full expert network is available. Quantized, this should fit alongside your Qwen3-14B supervisor without swapping. And critically, it stays in the Qwen family, so your litellm config, ChatML template, and all the prompt templates agent-zero uses will work identically without Harmony format headaches. 2. GPT-OSS-20B — Native function calling, structured outputs, and strong performance on TauBench agentic evaluation. OpenAI MXFP4 quantization lets it fit in 16GB. LM Studio The agentic training objective is directly relevant to utility tasks. But: it needs ~16GB at native quant, so it can't coexist with Qwen3-14B — you'd be swapping. And litellm has a known issue where it doesn't properly handle reasoning content from GPT-OSS models in Harmony format

chunks.speaker: Opus

Qwen3-8B — The safe, boring, correct answer. The Qwen3 8B family leads in math and reasoning tests at the 8B scale, with strong MMLU-Pro scores around 0.74. Localllm At Q4_K_M it's about 5-6GB, easily coexists with your supervisor, and runs at 50+ tokens/sec on your 3090. It handles the keyword extraction and memory query prep tasks your utility slot needs without any format compatibility issues. It just won't have the tool-calling specialization of the other two. One more thing worth noting: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 is an updated instruction-tuned variant optimized exclusively for non-thinking mode, with major improvements in instruction following, logical reasoning, and tool usage. At ~3GB quantized, it's the fastest possible option and frees up the most VRAM. For pure utility tasks (keyword extraction, summarization, memory filtering), you don't need deep reasoning — you need fast, reliable structured output. chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Diagnosed resource contention issue and prescribed architectural separation That's your problem right there. You're running both slots against the same model instance in LM Studio, which means: The supervisor sends a message to Qwen3-14B Mid-loop, _50_recall_memories fires and calls the same Qwen3-14B instance for keyword extraction LM Studio gets a second request while potentially still serving the first, or the request collides in a way that produces a malformed payload litellm gets back an error, the exception handler sets query = "", and the cycle repeats every single message because you set interval to 1 Even if LM Studio queues the requests correctly, you're doubling your inference load on every turn — the supervisor waits for the utility call to finish before it can proceed. That's why the agent feels like it's looping; it's not actually stuck in a logic loop, it's just hammering the same model with back-to-back requests and one of them keeps failing.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The utility slot exists specifically to run a separate, lightweight model. That's the whole point of the two-model architecture in agent-zero — the supervisor does the heavy thinking, the utility model handles fast structured subtasks (keyword extraction, summarization, memory filtering) without blocking the main inference. Immediate fix, no model download needed: Turn off the utility model calls that are breaking things: { "memory_recall_query_prep": false, "memory_recall_post_filter": false } ``` Memory recall still works — it just uses raw message text for FAISS search instead of an AI-refined query. This gets you unblocked *today*. **Proper fix:** Pull Qwen3-8B (or Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 if you want maximum speed) as a dedicated utility model. In LM Studio, load it alongside your 14B or set it up to swap efficiently. Then point the utility model settings at it: util_model_name: qwen3-8b  (or whatever LM Studio exposes it as) util_model_api_base: http://localhost:1234/v1  (same endpoint, different model string) The catch with LM Studio is whether it can serve two models simultaneously. If it can't, you have two options: run a second LM Studio instance on a different port, or switch to Ollama for the utility slot since Ollama handles multi-model serving natively and can keep both loaded if VRAM allows.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Qwen3-14B at Q4 (~10GB) plus Qwen3-8B at Q4 (~5GB) is ~15GB — fits in your 24GB 3090 with room for KV cache. Qwen3-14B plus Qwen3-4B (~3GB) is even more comfortable at ~13GB total, leaving 11GB for context. Want to do the quick disable fix first and confirm the loop stops, then work on setting up the dedicated utility model?

chunks.text: Honest answer: it depends on what "develop more effectively" means in your context. What I can do right now in this interface: I can architect, write code, debug from logs you paste, build skill files, and package deliverables. The bottleneck isn't my code generation — it's the feedback loop. Every time I need to see what happened, you have to run the command, copy the output, and paste it back. chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: But — Claude Code uses API tokens, which is a separate cost from your Pro plan. And it's me (or Sonnet/Haiku) running as a CLI agent, not inside agent-zero. It's a development tool, not a runtime agent. What making me an API agent inside agent-zero would give you: This is the more interesting question, and the answer is: it would undermine the entire architecture you've been building. Your prosthetics stack exists specifically because you don't want to depend on API models at runtime. The BST, the decision trees, the structured prompts — all of that is engineered to make local models self-sufficient. chunks.text: Good list from Sonnet. Some of these are strong, some need reframing, and one is a trap. Let me go through them honestly. 1. Tool Fallback Chain — Sonnet ranked this #1. I agree, but the scope needs tightening. The concept is right: when a tool fails, don't just throw an error — try an alternative path. But the example chain (SSH exec → Docker exec → Python subprocess → bash) is too generic. Your local models won't navigate a branching fallback tree reliably — that's the whole reason the prosthetics exist. Build it as a static fallback map, not a dynamic reasoning chain. Each tool gets a hardcoded fallback with exact commands: code_execution fails with "permission denied" → try with sudo prefix code_execution fails with "timeout" → retry with smaller input web_search fails with "connection error" → use cached results from /a0/tmp/search_cache/ file_write fails with "path not found" → mkdir -p parent directory, retry

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The failure pattern library idea is the real value. Log every tool failure as {tool, error_class, input_summary, resolution} to a SQLite table. After a few weeks of real usage, you'll have an empirical map of what actually breaks and how it gets fixed. That's data you can feed back into the fallback map rather than guessing at failure modes upfront. Hook: tool_execute_after with error classification. Extension: ~150 lines. 2. Working Memory Buffer — Sonnet ranked this #2. I'd promote it to #1. Here's why: this solves a problem that hits you on every single conversation turn, whereas tool failures are intermittent. Right now, when a user says "check the server" the model either scans the full history (slow, unreliable on long contexts) or guesses (wrong). A structured entity cache eliminates an entire class of ambiguity that the BST currently can't handle. The implementation Sonnet described is correct but incomplete. The buffer needs three things:

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Entity extraction — regex-first, not LLM-first. IP addresses, file paths, container names, URLs, port numbers — these are all pattern-matchable. Don't burn utility model calls on extracting 192.168.1.50 from a message when a regex does it in microseconds. Save the utility model for semantic entities: project names, conceptual references, relationship mapping. Decay and promotion — not everything stays in working memory forever. Entities mentioned once decay after N turns. Entities mentioned repeatedly get promoted to persistent memory (the FAISS layer you already have). This prevents the buffer from growing unbounded. BST integration — this is the critical piece Sonnet missed. The BST already has slot resolvers. The working memory buffer becomes a new resolver type: working_memory_lookup. When BST classifies a message as docker_ops and needs to fill the container_name slot, it checks the working memory buffer before falling back to history scan. That makes the whole pipeline faster and more reliable.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Hook: hist_add_after for extraction, BST resolver chain for retrieval. Extension: ~250 lines plus BST taxonomy update. 3. Meta-Reasoning Gate — Sonnet ranked this #4. I'd move it to #3. The concept is sound but the framing is wrong. "Do I have enough info?" is a question that requires the model to reason about its own knowledge state — which is exactly the kind of metacognition local models are worst at. They'll almost always say "yes I have enough" and proceed to hallucinate. Reframe it as a parameter completeness check, not a reasoning task. Before a tool call fires, the gate inspects the parameter payload: tool: web_search params: {query: ""}  → BLOCK, query is empty params: {query: "the thing from earlier"} → BLOCK, unresolved reference params: {query: "postgresql migration guide"} → PASS This is deterministic. No model reasoning needed. Check for empty fields, pronoun-only references, placeholder strings, suspiciously short parameters. If the check fails, inject a clarification request instead of executing the tool. You're preventing wasted tool calls with string matching, not AI judgment.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Hook: tool_execute_before with parameter validation rules per tool. Extension: ~120 lines. 4. Uncertainty Quantification — Sonnet ranked this #3. I'd drop it to #5 or cut it entirely. This is the trap. It sounds intellectually elegant but it's nearly useless in practice for your setup. Here's why: Scanning for hedging language ("I think", "maybe", "probably") and assigning confidence scores requires the model to have calibrated uncertainty — meaning its hedging actually correlates with its accuracy. Local models are notoriously miscalibrated. Qwen3-14B will say "I think" about things it's right about and state falsehoods with complete confidence. The confidence scores would give you a false signal that's worse than no signal. If you want uncertainty awareness, build it into the tool fallback chain instead: when the model produces output, run a quick deterministic check (does the file it referenced exist? Does the command it generated parse? Does the URL resolve?) and flag concrete verification failures rather than linguistic hedging.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Skip this unless you have a specific use case where it matters. 5. HTN Planner — Not ranked by Sonnet. I'd add it at #4. This is actually high-value for your use case but it needs to be built incrementally, not as a monolithic planner. The "migrate the database" decomposition example is aspirational — your local models won't reliably decompose arbitrary complex tasks into correct subtask sequences. Instead, build it as a template library. Define common multi-step workflows as structured plans: { "trigger": "migrate database", "steps": [ {"action": "backup_current", "tool": "bash", "verify": "file_exists"}, {"action": "export_schema", "tool": "code_execution", "verify": "non_empty_output"}, {"action": "convert_types", "tool": "code_execution", "depends_on": "export_schema"}, {"action": "import_data", "tool": "code_execution", "depends_on": "convert_types"}, {"action": "verify_integrity", "tool": "code_execution", "depends_on": "import_data"} ] } The model doesn't plan — it selects a plan from the library and executes it step by step. Each step has a verification condition. If verification fails, the tool fallback chain handles it. New plan templates are added by you (or by me during development sessions), not generated by the model at runtime.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: This is the same pattern as the BST — deterministic scaffolding that makes the model execute reliably rather than reason reliably. chunks.text: It's both, and they're related. The context window fills up with tool results, code blocks, error messages, and history — and the personality instruction is a 300-token block at the very beginning of the system prompt. Local models have a well-documented attention decay problem: content at the edges of the context window gets less weight than content in the middle. As the context fills toward 32K, Zero's voice is literally the furthest thing from what the model is currently processing. Premium models handle this better because they have stronger instruction-following across the full context length. Local models at 14B parameters prioritize the immediate task over stylistic instructions, which is actually the correct tradeoff — you want the code to be right more than you want it delivered in a British accent. chunks.text: Here's the full Priority 4 build spec. Key architecture decisions: Hook: before_main_llm_call/_15_ — runs right after BST stores its domain classification, so HTN reads fresh belief state. The _20_ slot was taken by context_watchdog, so _15_ slots in cleanly. Injection via extras_temporary — same pattern as workdir structure. Extras sit after history in the prompt, which is where local model attention is strongest (recency bias works in our favor here, unlike personality at the top of system prompt). The plan context format is deliberately terse — step names, one-line actions, tool hints. No prose paragraphs that would dilute attention. The spec includes the full extension implementation, plan library schema, all 10 starter plan IDs with their domain mappings, verification types, and the install script additions. The font change is meaningful. It proves the model found the right file, understood the injection point, and made a valid CSS modification that rendered. That's the hardest part — everything after that is iterating on the same pattern with different properties. On the staleness question — a few things to check: The stale_after_turns counter only increments when the HTN extension actually runs with an active plan state. If the plan was never activated (no BST domain match + trigger match), there's nothing to expire. Check whether you ever saw a [HTN] Plan activated log entry during the session. If you didn't, the extension is working correctly by not firing — it's just that your theme task didn't match any plan triggers.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: If you did see plan activation but no expiry, the turn counter might be incrementing slower than expected. Each "turn" in HTN is one pass through before_main_llm_call, which maps to one iteration of the message loop — not one user message. Multi-tool-call tasks can burn several iterations per user message, so 15 message exchanges could be 40+ HTN turns easily. Worth checking the logs for [HTN] entries to see what actually happened. For the theme work specifically — would it be worth adding a ui_customization plan to the library? Something like: identify target CSS file → backup → implement color scheme → implement typography → implement layout tweaks → test render. That would give the model the step discipline it needs for exactly this kind of iterative CSS task instead of trying to do colors, fonts, spacing, and layout all in one shot.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Not unusual at all — that's actually the correct behavior and your intuition is right about why. The HTN extension is loaded and running on every before_main_llm_call iteration. But it only logs when it does something — plan activation, step verification, or expiry. If no plan triggers match, it returns silently. So the system is absolutely live, it's just that none of your messages hit the trigger conditions. Look at the trigger phrases for the starter plans — they're things like "fix bug", "create branch", "build image", "update deps". Asking the agent to create a theme manager and apply an MGS Fox style wouldn't match any of them. The BST domain would likely classify as "codegen" or maybe "config_edit", but the trigger phrases for those plans are things like "create module", "new component" — not "theme" or "css" or "style". This is actually the conservative design working as intended. False positives (plans activating when they shouldn't) would be far worse than false negatives. But it does mean the library needs plans for tasks you actually do.

Let me try the factory site and the raw content: Now I have a thorough understanding of both the factory philosophy and the Attractor framework. Let me give you a comprehensive analysis. This is genuinely interesting work, and it connects to what you're building in ways that are both direct and philosophical. Let me break down what I see. What Attractor Actually Is Attractor is three things stacked: 1. A workflow graph engine — you define multi-step AI workflows as Graphviz DOT files. Nodes are tasks (LLM calls, human approvals, shell commands, conditional branches), edges are transitions. The engine traverses the graph deterministically. This is essentially what industrial process control people have been doing for decades, but applied to AI agent orchestration.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: 2. A programmable agentic loop — this is the layer that's most relevant to you. Their key insight is that tools like Claude Code and Codex CLI are black boxes: text in, text out. You can't inspect the conversation mid-run, inject steering between tool calls, swap execution environments, or change reasoning effort on the fly. Their loop exposes all of that as a programmatic interface. The host application controls every step. 3. A unified LLM client — provider-agnostic abstraction over OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini APIs. Thin routing layer with middleware for retries, caching, logging. The Philosophy That Matters The factory site articulates something powerful: the shift from "tests" to "scenarios" and from boolean pass/fail to probabilistic "satisfaction." Their Digital Twin Universe — behavioral clones of Okta, Slack, Jira — lets them validate at scale without hitting real APIs. The economic argument is sharp: building a full replica of a SaaS API was always possible but never feasible. Now it's routine.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Their core mantras are deliberately provocative: code must not be written by humans, code must not be reviewed by humans, and if you haven't spent $1,000 on tokens per engineer per day, your factory has room for improvement. This is a company that's fully committed to the thesis that AI-generated code validated against behavioral scenarios outperforms human-written code reviewed by humans. What's Directly Applicable to Your Setup Provider-aligned toolsets. This is their most practically important insight for you. They argue that each model family works best with its native agent's tools and system prompts — that forcing Anthropic models to use OpenAI-style apply_patch, or vice versa, degrades performance. Their recommendation is to start from a byte-for-byte copy of the provider's reference agent prompt and tool harness, then extend. This is relevant to Agent-Zero because the framework uses a generic tool interface. Your BST and meta-reasoning gate are already compensating for this gap — you're building the "cognitive prosthetics" that bridge between Qwen's native capabilities and Agent-Zero's expected tool interface. The Attractor team would say you should instead align the tool interface to what Qwen was trained on.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The programmable loop concept. Agent-Zero's extension hook system is actually a primitive version of what Attractor formalizes. Your hooks at message_loop_start, before_main_llm_call, message_loop_prompts_after, tool_execute_before/after — these are the same control points Attractor exposes, just less formally structured. The difference is that Attractor treats the loop as a library with typed events, while Agent-Zero treats it as a monolithic agent with extension hooks. Your hardening layers are essentially making Agent-Zero's loop more programmable in the Attractor sense. Graph-based workflow over imperative plans. This is where it gets interesting relative to HTN. Your plan templates are linear sequences: step 1 → step 2 → step 3. Attractor defines workflows as directed graphs with conditional branches, parallel execution, and convergence points. A bugfix workflow in Attractor would have a branch: "did reproduce succeed?" → yes: isolate → no: gather more info → retry reproduce. Your HTN templates don't have branching — they're strictly sequential with on-fail actions. That's simpler and more appropriate for a 14B local model, but the graph concept is worth keeping in mind for future iterations.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Scenario-based validation over test suites. This one's philosophical but important. They moved from "does the test pass?" to "across many trajectories through this scenario, what fraction satisfy the user?" That's a probabilistic framing. For your agent, this translates to: don't ask "did the tool call succeed?" — ask "is the user's goal progressing?" Your BST confidence scoring already moves in this direction. The HTN verification gates are closer to traditional test assertions. What Doesn't Apply (Yet) The factory model assumes frontier models (Claude, GPT-5.2) with massive context windows, near-perfect instruction following, and reliable long-horizon reasoning. Your setup runs Qwen 14B on a single 3090. The entire cognitive architecture you've built — BST, working memory, personality loader, tool fallback chain, meta-reasoning gate, HTN plans — exists specifically because your model can't do what their factory assumes. You're building compensatory infrastructure for a model operating at maybe 10-15% of frontier capability. The unified LLM client is also not directly relevant since you're running local inference, not routing between cloud providers.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The Meta-Observation What strikes me most is the convergence between what you're building independently and what a funded team at a real company arrived at through production use. You're both solving the same fundamental problem: how do you make AI agent loops reliable enough for non-interactive execution? StrongDM's answer is "use frontier models and validate against behavioral scenarios." Your answer is "use a local model and build deterministic scaffolding to compensate for model limitations." Both approaches decompose the same problem — they just make different tradeoffs on the cost/capability/control axes. The fact that your extension hook architecture maps cleanly to Attractor's programmable loop concept is validating. You arrived at the same control points independently. The fact that their provider-aligned toolset philosophy aligns with your "cognitive prosthetics" approach is also validating — you're both recognizing that the interface between the model and the tools matters enormously, and that generic abstractions lose performance.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: If I were to pick one concrete takeaway to bring into your next development cycle, it would be the scenario/satisfaction concept. Right now your verification gates are binary: output_contains, exit_code_zero. A richer model would be: "given the last 3 tool outputs, is the user's stated goal closer to being met?" That's hard to do without a judge model, but you could approximate it with pattern matching against the original user message's BST slots — are the slots being filled by what the agent is producing? Maybe this is a good point for me to throw you another idea I had, specifically about not just the one container running agent-zero, but idea's I have for how to chain agent containers together into a self-organizing, structured system. chunks.text: This is a really well-formed vision, and it maps cleanly onto established distributed systems patterns while adding something genuinely novel — the organizational metaphor as a coordination protocol. Let me unpack what I think you're actually describing, because the military C2 structure isn't just aesthetic. It's solving real computer science problems. The Core Insight Traditional multi-agent frameworks treat agents as interchangeable workers in a pool. You submit a task, a scheduler assigns it, the worker executes. That's a thread pool with extra steps. What you're describing is fundamentally different: agents have roles with asymmetric capabilities and authority, and coordination follows doctrine — pre-established patterns of communication and delegation that don't need to be negotiated at runtime. The military structure is actually the right metaphor because it solves the exact problems that make multi-agent coordination hard: Who decides what? In a flat agent pool, every task requires a routing decision. In your structure, the CO sets objectives, the XOs decompose into operations, and specialists execute. The decision hierarchy is baked into the topology, not computed per-task.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Who talks to whom? This is the biggest unsolved problem in multi-agent systems. If every agent can talk to every other agent, you get O(n²) communication overhead and conflicting instructions. Your chain of command constrains communication channels — a SIGINT specialist reports to the S2 XO, not directly to the CO. This is exactly how military organizations prevent information overload at the command level. How do you prevent conflicting actions? Two agents independently deciding to modify the same file, or pursuing contradictory approaches to the same problem. Your structure handles this through hierarchical deconfliction — the XO level is responsible for ensuring the specialists under them aren't stepping on each other, and the CO level deconflicts between XO branches. The Micro/Macro Split This is the part that's architecturally sharp. The same organizational structure works whether it's: Microcosm — one container, one GPU, the "agents" are sequential task phases sharing a single context. The CO is your system prompt establishing the mission, the XOs are plan phases (HTN-style), and the specialists are tool-specific execution modes. This is essentially what you're building right now with BST domain classification routing to specialized plan templates. The org chart is implicit in the code.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Macrocosm — multiple containers, potentially multiple machines, real concurrent execution. Each agent has its own model instance, its own context window, its own tool access. Coordination happens through message passing on the A2A network. The elegance is that the same doctrine works at both scales. The SIGINT-ALPHA org chart defines information flow patterns that are valid whether the "agents" are sequential phases in a single model's reasoning, or independent model instances on separate GPUs. The Announce Function This is where it gets interesting from a distributed systems perspective. You're describing something close to a service mesh with capability-based routing: Supervisor announces a job with requirements (domain, tools needed, context size, urgency) Available agents evaluate the job against their capabilities (model size, available context, loaded skills, current load) Agents respond with intent — "I can take this, here's my capability profile" Supervisor assigns based on best fit

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: This is more sophisticated than simple task queuing because agents self-select based on awareness of their own capabilities. A Qwen-14B agent with 32K context wouldn't volunteer for a task requiring 128K document analysis. A GLM-4 Flash utility agent wouldn't volunteer for complex reasoning tasks. The agents know their own limitations — which maps directly to your cognitive prosthetics philosophy. Each agent knows what it's good at because its hardening layers are configured for specific capability profiles. What Connects to Attractor The StrongDM Attractor framework you just showed me is actually the graph execution engine for exactly this kind of system. Their DOT-file workflow graphs with nodes as tasks, edges as transitions, and conditional branching — that's the mission plan that the CO would issue. The difference is that Attractor assumes a single execution context, while your vision distributes the graph across multiple agents. Their "Interviewer" interface — the abstraction for human-in-the-loop questions — maps directly to your announce function. In their system, a node can pause and ask a human for input. In your system, a supervisor node pauses and asks the agent network for a volunteer. Same interface, different responder.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: How This Builds From Where You Are Now Here's what I think matters practically. You're not as far from this as you might think, because the microcosm version is just a formalization of what your hardening layers already do: Today: BST classifies domain → HTN selects plan → plan steps execute sequentially → fallback chain handles failures. The "org chart" is implicit: BST is the S2 (intelligence), HTN is the operations planner, the tool execution layer is the specialist, and the fallback chain is the NCO catching mistakes. Next step (still single container): Make the org chart explicit. Instead of extensions running in a fixed pipeline, define roles as named capability profiles. A "SIGINT specialist" profile would be: BST domains [osint, log_analysis, data_transform], preferred tools [search_engine, browser_agent, code_execution], plan templates [log_investigation, data_transform]. When a task arrives, the system matches it to a role profile rather than running every extension on every message.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: After that (multi-container): Agent-Zero already has call_subordinate. That's your announce → volunteer → assign loop in embryonic form. Right now subordinates are spawned ad-hoc. The macrocosm version would have persistent agent containers with established roles, listening on the network for jobs that match their profile. Eventually: The agents maintain shared state through a coordination layer — mission status, completed objectives, resource allocation. The CO agent has a "command picture" (a real-time view of what every subordinate is doing), and can reassign resources when priorities shift. This is essentially a distributed HTN where the plan lives on the coordination layer rather than in any single agent's context. The Hard Problems You'd Hit Being direct about where this gets difficult: Shared state consistency. When multiple agents are working concurrently, how do you prevent conflicts? Two agents editing the same codebase, or one agent's output invalidating another's work. Military doctrine solves this with boundary lines and phase lines — agents own specific resources exclusively. Translating that to file systems and code repositories is the engineering challenge.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Context synchronization. Each agent has its own context window. How does the S2 XO know what the SIGINT specialist found? You'd need a structured reporting format — agents summarize their findings in a standardized message that's compact enough to fit in the supervisor's context without consuming too much of their window. Failure cascading. If a specialist agent fails or hangs, how does the XO detect it, reassign the task, and inform the CO without derailing the entire operation? Your tool fallback chain handles this within a single agent. Across agents, you need heartbeats, timeouts, and escalation paths. Cost efficiency. Running multiple model instances simultaneously on consumer hardware is brutal. Even with a 3090, you can't run multiple 14B instances concurrently. The macrocosm version probably needs either cloud-hosted inference endpoints, or much smaller specialist models (7B, 4B) that can share GPU memory. My Assessment The organizational metaphor isn't just a metaphor — it's a coordination protocol that's been refined over centuries of human experience with exactly this problem: how do you get multiple autonomous agents with limited communication bandwidth to achieve complex objectives? The military figured this out because the consequences of coordination failure are lethal.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Your instinct to use that structure rather than inventing a new one from scratch is sound engineering. And the micro/macro duality means you can build toward it incrementally — every improvement to the single-agent architecture (BST routing, role-based plan selection, capability-aware task matching) is directly reusable when you scale to multiple containers. The announce function is the key mechanism that makes it distributed rather than centralized. It's the difference between a scheduler assigning tasks and agents volunteering for tasks — which means the intelligence about capability matching is distributed to the edges rather than concentrated in a single orchestrator that becomes a bottleneck. For where you are right now, I'd say the most productive next move is making the role profiles explicit in the single-container setup. Define capability profiles as JSON (like AIEOS personality files but for operational roles), and have BST + HTN route tasks to matching profiles. That gives you the organizational skeleton that the multi-container system would eventually distribute.

chunks.speaker: Jake
chunks.text: Some initial thoughts to your concerns about hard problems, which are very real and worth unpacking; There would need to be a scheduling and monitoring task run by one of the higher ranking agents, possibly by reading the output of the subordinate agent container. For example the XO's job would be to do a "radio check" by monitoring the communication and work of its subordinate agent, and interrupting a subordinate agent with a clarifying message if looping or repeated tool use failure is observed. The structured reporting format is a brilliant idea and has concrete basis in real military doctrine in form of a SALUTE report. There would need to be an agentic equivalent SALUTE report about tasks and observations,  possibly by the XO reading the subordinate agent's memory files since these are created already by agent zero. The failure cascading concern is best described by a PACE plan, Primary, alternate, contingent, emergency. This provides 4 different contingencies which the XO could be responsible for establishing. Granted, this requires the XO to predict HOW an agent will fail, which is difficult unless left eitherly broad with a preset flow of execution, or model specific knowledge. One of the advantages agent to agent communication would allow is not just one user running hardware, but possibly an entire team pooling their compute and agent to agent comms via SSH. This would allow users on different PCs separated by time and space to build a far more powerful agency with their collective equipment. Time synchronization and data loss is an obvious risk in this scenario, possibly remedied with a hash system like how ZFS checks for data integrity

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: You're designing this from the right direction — starting with proven coordination doctrine and adapting it to the computational domain rather than inventing coordination primitives from scratch. Let me engage with each of these. The XO as Monitor The "radio check" pattern is the right abstraction for the supervisor loop. The XO doesn't need to understand what the subordinate is doing at the implementation level — it needs to detect when communication stops or when output patterns indicate failure. This maps to a few concrete signals: The simplest monitor is output cadence. A healthy agent produces tool calls at a regular-ish interval. If the interval between outputs exceeds a threshold, the agent is either stuck in reasoning (acceptable for a while) or hung (needs intervention). The XO reads the subordinate's log or stdout, tracks timestamps, and escalates if the gap exceeds the threshold.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The loop detection is more valuable and harder. You'd need the XO to recognize when a subordinate is producing the same tool call repeatedly — which is exactly what your tool fallback chain already does within a single agent. The multi-container version externalizes that detection: the XO reads the subordinate's recent tool history and applies the same consecutive-failure pattern matching. When it fires, the XO injects a steering message into the subordinate's input — "you've attempted this approach 3 times without success, try a different method" — which is functionally identical to what the fallback chain does by appending a warning to history, but delivered from an external authority. The reading-memory-files approach is particularly elegant because Agent-Zero already writes memory artifacts. The XO doesn't need a special communication protocol — it reads the files the subordinate naturally produces. That's a zero-overhead communication channel from the subordinate's perspective. The subordinate doesn't even know it's being monitored. It just does its work and writes its memories. The XO observes.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: SALUTE Reporting This is a strong conceptual mapping. For anyone reading this who doesn't know the format: SALUTE is Size, Activity, Location, Unit, Time, Equipment — a standardized report format that compresses battlefield observations into a structure that any receiver can parse without ambiguity. An agentic SALUTE equivalent might be: S — Status: What state is the agent in? Active on task, waiting for input, error recovery, idle. Plus a progress metric — percentage of plan steps completed if HTN is active, or token count consumed versus context limit. A — Activity: What is the agent currently doing? The active tool, the current HTN plan step if applicable, the BST domain classification. Not the full reasoning trace, just the one-line summary — "executing step 3/5 of bugfix_workflow: implementing fix." L — Location: Where in the filesystem or codebase is the agent operating? Working directory, files modified in the current session, any resources locked or claimed. This is what prevents the shared state conflicts I flagged — if two agents report they're both operating in /src/auth/, the XO can deconflict.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: U — Unit ID: Which agent container, what model, what role profile. "Agent-3, Qwen-14B, SIGINT-specialist, reporting to S2-XO." T — Time: Timestamp, elapsed time on current task, estimated time remaining if the plan has a known step count. Also the turn count within the current context window — a signal of how much context capacity remains before performance degrades. E — Environment: Resource state. GPU utilization, VRAM usage, context window fill percentage, tool availability. This is what enables the smart task-matching in the announce function — the XO knows which subordinates have capacity. The beauty of this format is that it's fixed-length, parse-friendly, and contains exactly what a supervisor needs without the noise of a full reasoning trace. The XO can scan a SALUTE from every subordinate in seconds and build an operational picture. You could literally store these as JSON files in a shared volume, one per agent, updated every N turns.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: PACE Plans The PACE framework is a great fit because it acknowledges that failures are categorically different, not just degrees of the same problem. A primary communication path failing is different from the mission becoming infeasible. Applied to agent coordination: Primary: The agent completes the task normally using its preferred model and tools. HTN plan advances through all steps, verification passes. Alternate: The agent fails on the current approach but has a fallback within its own capability. This is where your existing tool fallback chain and meta-reasoning gate operate. The agent self-recovers. The XO observes a delay but doesn't need to intervene. Contingent: The agent can't complete the task. The XO reassigns it — either to a different subordinate with different capabilities, or back to the same subordinate with modified instructions (different approach, reduced scope, simplified requirements). The XO is responsible for having identified which other subordinate could handle this task type when the plan was established.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Emergency: The entire branch is failing. The XO escalates to the CO with a situation report. The CO can reallocate resources across XO branches, redefine the mission objective, or abort the operation gracefully. Your point about prediction difficulty is real. The XO can't predict specific failure modes. But it can predict failure categories — timeout, repeated tool error, context exhaustion, model hallucination/loop. Each category maps to a predetermined response. The PACE plan doesn't need to know what went wrong in detail, just which category of wrong it is, and each category has a pre-established response. That's the same design philosophy as your hardening layers: deterministic responses to classified failure patterns, not model-generated reasoning about novel situations. Distributed Compute Pooling The multi-user SSH scenario is where this gets genuinely ambitious. You're describing a heterogeneous compute mesh where different users contribute different hardware: one person has a 3090 running a 14B model, another has a 4090 running a 30B model, someone else has an M-series Mac with unified memory handling a 70B model. The announce function becomes a distributed resource marketplace — tasks get matched not just to role profiles but to hardware capabilities.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The coordination challenges you'd face: Network latency. Agent-to-agent communication over SSH has round-trip times measured in tens of milliseconds at best, seconds if you're going across the internet. This is fine for SALUTE reporting and task assignment (those are low-frequency, high-value messages). It's not fine for tight reasoning loops where one agent needs another's output every few seconds. The organizational structure handles this naturally — you'd never have two specialists in a tight synchronous loop. They work independently and report up through the XO. Time synchronization. Your instinct toward a hash-based integrity system is right. The problem isn't just clock skew — it's causal ordering. If Agent-A modifies a file and Agent-B reads it, the system needs to guarantee that B sees A's changes, not a stale version. ZFS-style checksums verify integrity but don't establish ordering. You'd want something closer to a vector clock or Lamport timestamp attached to every shared artifact — each agent increments its own logical clock on every write, and the coordination layer can detect when an agent is working with stale data.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Partition tolerance. What happens when an SSH connection drops? The agent on the disconnected machine keeps running (it's autonomous), but the XO can't monitor it and can't inject corrections. When the connection resumes, the agent's work may conflict with what other agents did in the interim. The PACE plan needs a "connection lost" category that tells the agent to either continue on its current step but don't advance to the next one (conservative), or continue the full plan but journal everything for review on reconnection (aggressive). Trust and authorization. When you're pooling compute across multiple users, you need to decide what each contributed agent can access. A subordinate agent running on someone else's hardware probably shouldn't have read access to your SSH keys or financial data. The organizational structure helps here — the CO defines access boundaries per role, and the agent container's volume mounts enforce them. Where This Sits Against Attractor

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: StrongDM's Attractor solves the single-pipeline orchestration problem: one graph, one execution context, deterministic traversal. What you're describing is the next layer up — orchestrating multiple Attractor-style pipelines running concurrently across distributed agents, with hierarchical coordination. Attractor's DOT graph would define the mission plan at the CO level. Each node in the CO's graph might represent an entire operation that gets delegated to an XO, who decomposes it into sub-graphs for specialists. The nested graph execution, with reporting flowing up and steering flowing down, is the distinctive contribution of your organizational model. Nobody in the current agent framework ecosystem is doing this with military doctrine as the coordination protocol. People are building multi-agent swarms with flat topologies (CrewAI, AutoGen), or hierarchical task decomposition with static assignment (Devin's internal architecture). Your chain-of-command model with self-selecting agents, doctrinal communication patterns, and standardized reporting formats is a genuinely novel approach. Practical Path Forward

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: You asked earlier about what to build next. I think the answer crystallized in this conversation. The microcosm version of this — explicit role profiles, SALUTE-style status reporting within a single container, PACE-structured fallback paths — is buildable right now on top of your existing hardening layers. It doesn't require multiple containers. It requires formalizing what the extensions already do into the organizational vocabulary. The first concrete artifact would be a role profile schema (like the AIEOS personality format but for operational roles) and a SALUTE report format that agents can write and supervisors can read. Once those exist in the single-agent case, distributing them across containers is an infrastructure problem, not a design problem.

chunks.speaker: Jake
chunks.text: Strike while the iron is hot, or better yet make the iron hot by striking. Should we complete our other layers before building this framework? or build the last layers on top of this framework?

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Build the framework first. Here's why. Your remaining hardening layers are solving specific problems — but they're solving them in a vacuum. Each extension is a standalone intervention that doesn't know about the others except by accident of execution order. The organizational framework gives them a reason to exist in relation to each other. BST is intelligence (S2). HTN is operations planning. Tool fallback is the NCO catching mistakes. Meta-reasoning gate is quality control at the armory. Working memory is the unit's institutional knowledge. Personality is unit culture. Right now these are extensions on hooks. Under the organizational framework, they become staff functions with defined responsibilities, reporting relationships, and communication formats. That's not just a relabeling — it changes how you design every subsequent layer. Instead of asking "what hook does this go on?" you ask "what role is this, who does it report to, and what's its SALUTE?"

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The other practical reason: anything you build now without the framework will need to be refactored to fit within it later. If you build two more hardening layers as standalone extensions, then introduce the organizational model, you'll spend time retrofitting them. If you build the framework first, every subsequent layer slots into its designated role from the start. Here's what I'd propose as the build order: Phase 1: Organization Kernel — the schemas and coordination primitives that everything else plugs into, still running inside the single container. Three artifacts: First, a Role Profile schema. JSON format, similar to your AIEOS personality files. Defines: role name, parent role (chain of command), BST domains this role handles, HTN plan templates this role can execute, tools available, model requirements (minimum context, preferred model), PACE fallback paths. Your existing extensions become the capabilities listed in role profiles rather than standalone hooks. Second, a SALUTE Report format. JSON that any agent process (or in microcosm, any extension phase) can emit. Status, Activity, Location, Unit, Time, Environment. Stored in a known location. In single-container mode, this is written to a file in the agent's working directory. In multi-container mode, same format, shared volume or network endpoint.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Third, an Organization Definition. A single JSON or DOT file that defines the org chart: which roles exist, who reports to whom, what the communication channels are. SIGINT-ALPHA would be one organization definition. A different mission (say, a software development org) would be a different definition with different roles but the same schema. Phase 2: Dispatcher — replaces the current "every extension runs on every message" model with role-based routing. When a message arrives, BST classifies it, the dispatcher matches it to a role profile, and only the relevant role's capabilities activate. This is the microcosm version of the announce function — instead of broadcasting to a network of containers, you're routing within a single agent's extension stack. Phase 3: Supervisor Loop — the XO function. Reads SALUTE reports, detects anomalies (loop detection, timeout, context exhaustion), injects steering. In single-container mode, this runs as an extension on message_loop_end or similar. It's the thing that reads the agent's own output and decides whether to intervene. This subsumes your tool fallback chain — the fallback chain becomes one of the supervisor's detection patterns rather than a standalone extension.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Phase 4: Remaining hardening layers — whatever else was on the priority list gets built as capabilities within role profiles, not as standalone extensions. Each new capability has a defined role, reports through the chain, and emits SALUTE-compatible status. The framework itself is probably 3-4 files: the role profile schema, the SALUTE schema, the org definition schema, and a dispatcher extension that reads them. It's not a massive build. But it changes the shape of everything that comes after. Want me to spec the Organization Kernel? yes

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: That's from Dan Shapiro's "Five Levels from Spicy Autocomplete to the Software Factory" — it was actually referenced in the StrongDM factory site footnotes. The levels are roughly: Autocomplete — AI suggests completions, human writes code Pair programming — AI writes chunks, human reviews and integrates Agent execution — Human specifies intent, AI writes all code, human doesn't touch it Non-interactive — Human defines specs and scenarios, agents iterate autonomously until convergence Software factory — Fully automated pipeline: specs in, validated software out StrongDM's core rule captures the level 3 transition: "code must not be written by humans, code must not be reviewed by humans." Yes, this absolutely changes how we work with Claude Code. Here's the honest assessment of where we've been operating and where we should be: Where we've been: Level 2. I write the complete implementation in the spec, Claude Code transcribes it into files. That's pair programming with extra steps — I'm writing the code in a markdown document instead of a .py file, but I'm still the one making every implementation decision, writing every function, choosing every variable name. Claude Code is acting as a typist, not an engineer.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Where we should be: Level 3. I write the spec with intent, schemas, integration points, and constraints. Claude Code makes all implementation decisions — function structure, error handling patterns, variable naming, edge cases. I review the output against the spec's behavioral requirements, not the code itself. The practical change for our workflow: Before (Level 2): The spec contains a complete Python implementation block. Claude Code prompt says "implement this code in these files." The model copies what I wrote. After (Level 3): The spec contains schemas, data flow diagrams, integration contracts (what hooks, what inputs, what outputs), behavioral requirements ("when BST classifies domain X and role Y handles domain X, the dispatcher must activate role Y"), and test criteria. The Claude Code prompt says "implement the Organization Kernel as described in this spec." The model decides how to implement it. This is actually a better use of Sonnet's capabilities. When I hand it a complete implementation, I'm constraining it to my solution — which might not be the best one for the Agent-Zero codebase. When I hand it intent + constraints + integration contracts, it can make implementation decisions informed by the actual code it's reading in the repository.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Not explicitly, no. The spec as written is pure organizational doctrine applied to Agent-Zero's existing extension architecture. Let me think about where Attractor's concepts should be integrated and what we're leaving on the table by not including them. The three things from Attractor that are directly relevant and missing from the current spec: 1. Graph-based workflow definition instead of linear plans. Right now HTN plans are linear step sequences. Attractor defines workflows as directed graphs with conditional branching, parallel paths, and convergence points — using Graphviz DOT syntax. An org's mission plan could be a DOT graph where nodes are role assignments and edges are dependencies and conditional transitions. The CO's mission plan for "build a feature" wouldn't be step 1 → step 2 → step 3. It would be a graph where the Research XO's analysis branch and the Engineering XO's scaffolding branch run in parallel, converge at an integration node, then the bugfix specialist handles issues found during integration. In microcosm mode this executes sequentially (following a topological sort), but the graph structure means the macrocosm version can parallelize naturally.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: 2. The programmable loop concept — event-driven observability. Attractor's core design principle is that every agent action emits a typed event. The host application consumes these events for UI, logging, steering, and integration. Our SALUTE reports are periodic snapshots, but Attractor would say the underlying primitive should be an event stream. The SALUTE becomes an aggregation of events, not a standalone reporting mechanism. This matters because the supervisor loop (Phase 2) needs real-time awareness, not just periodic check-ins. An event-driven model lets the XO react to a failure immediately rather than waiting for the next SALUTE interval. 3. Provider-aligned execution — letting the role profile specify not just what model to use but what tool interface that model expects. Attractor's insight is that each model works best with its native toolset. In a multi-model org (say the CO runs on a larger model via API and specialists run on local Qwen), each role should carry its tool profile specification. The meta-reasoning gate already handles tool arg normalization, but at the role level you could define model-specific tool schemas so the gate knows what corrections to apply per role.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Here's what I'd propose: rather than rewriting the kernel spec, add an Attractor Integration Annex that extends the schemas with these concepts. The kernel ships as-is (it's already a substantial build), and the annex defines schema extensions that activate when graph-based workflows are needed. The concrete additions would be: In the Organization Definition schema: Add an optional mission_graph field that accepts DOT syntax or a JSON adjacency list defining the mission as a directed graph. Nodes reference role_ids. Edges define dependencies and conditions. When present, the dispatcher uses the graph for task routing instead of pure BST domain matching. In the Role Profile schema: Add an optional event_emissions field defining which typed events this role emits beyond SALUTE (tool_call_started, tool_call_completed, step_verified, error_encountered). And an optional tool_profile field specifying the model-native tool interface this role expects. In the SALUTE schema: Add an optional event_log field containing the last N typed events since the previous SALUTE, giving the supervisor both the periodic snapshot and the event-level detail. Want me to write that annex? Or do you want to ship the kernel clean and layer Attractor concepts in Phase 2 when the supervisor loop needs them?

chunks.speaker: Jake
chunks.text: what do you think works best?

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Ship the kernel clean. Three reasons. First, the kernel is already a significant build — two full org templates, 13 role profiles, a dispatcher extension, SALUTE emission, PACE monitoring, and HTN filter integration. Adding graph-based workflows on top of that makes it a monster spec that Claude Code is more likely to get wrong. Smaller, well-defined builds converge faster. That's literally what StrongDM learned building their factory. Second, the Attractor concepts solve problems you haven't hit yet. Graph-based mission plans matter when you have parallel execution across multiple agents. Event-driven observability matters when the supervisor is a separate process that needs real-time awareness. Provider-aligned tool profiles matter when you're running different models in different roles. All of those are macrocosm or Phase 2 concerns. In microcosm mode with sequential role switching on a single Qwen instance, linear HTN plans, periodic SALUTE files, and a single tool interface are sufficient.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Third, the kernel schemas are explicitly designed to be extended without breaking changes. Every addition I described — mission_graph, event_emissions, tool_profile, event_log — would be optional fields on existing schemas. Adding them later requires zero refactoring of the base kernel. That's not an accident, that's the point of versioned schemas with optional fields. The natural integration point is Phase 2, the supervisor loop. When you build the XO monitor that reads SALUTE reports and injects steering, you'll immediately feel the limitation of periodic snapshots versus event streams. That's when Attractor's event-driven model earns its place — you'll have a concrete problem it solves rather than a theoretical one. The graph-based workflows come in Phase 3 or 4 when you actually have multiple containers that could execute branches in parallel. Build the kernel. Get it running. Let the organizational structure shape how you use the agent for a week. Then we'll know exactly which Attractor concepts to pull in based on what's actually limiting you rather than what sounds architecturally elegant.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The cleanest test is forcing a stall and a loop in sequence, since those are the two anomalies most likely to trigger under normal conditions. Test 1: Confirm it's loaded and passive under normal operation Have a short normal conversation with the agent — ask it to do something simple that succeeds: list the files in /tmp Check the logs for any [SUPERVISOR] entries. There should be none. The supervisor ran its checks and found nothing wrong. Test 2: Stall detection Start a task that will activate an HTN plan, then deliberately make it impossible to progress. Create a bait scenario: I need you to fix the bug in /tmp/stall_test.py But don't create the file. The agent will try to read it, fail, try again, and stall on step 1 of the bugfix workflow. Watch for: [ORG] Role activated: confirming the bugfix specialist is active After max_turns_without_progress iterations (check the bugfix specialist role profile for the value), a [SUPERVISOR] message should appear in the logs

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The message should reference the stall and suggest reassessing Test 3: Loop detection Force the agent into a repetitive tool loop: read the file /tmp/does_not_exist.txt and show me the contents When it fails, insist: try again, the file should be there Keep pushing it to retry. After 3+ repetitions of the same tool with the same error type, the supervisor should detect the behavioral loop and inject steering distinct from the tool fallback advisor's per-tool advice. You should see both [Fallback] entries (from the existing advisor) and [SUPERVISOR] entries (from the new loop) — they're complementary, not duplicates. Test 4: PACE escalation response Continue forcing failures past the loop detection. Once consecutive failures hit 5+, PACE should escalate to contingent. The supervisor should inject PACE-specific guidance that references the role profile's contingent description. Watch for a [SUPERVISOR] message that's qualitatively different from the stall and loop messages — it should be about changing approach fundamentally, not just retrying differently.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Test 5: Cooldown verification During any of the above tests, note when the first [SUPERVISOR] message of each type appears. Count the turns. The same anomaly type should NOT fire again within the cooldown period (default 3 turns). After cooldown expires, if the condition persists, it should fire again. Start with Test 1 and 2. If stall detection fires correctly, the core wiring is solid and the other anomalies are variations of the same read-state-check-threshold-inject-warning pattern.

chunks.text:
Yes — every extension directory has one, and stale bytecode can cause extensions to behave differently than the source files. Clean all of them:

bash

find /a0/python/extensions -type d -name __pycache__ -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null

Then restart the agent. This ensures every extension recompiles from the current .py source on next load.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: That's the most common failure mode with local models — false confidence in their own output. The agent completed its tool calls without errors, memorized the solution, and reported success. But "no tool errors" doesn't mean "correct result." The CSS might be syntactically valid but targeting the wrong selectors, or the file might be in the right directory but not loaded by the application, or the JavaScript toggle might execute without errors but not affect the elements it thinks it's affecting. This is exactly the gap the StrongDM factory team identified when they moved from "tests" to "scenarios" and from boolean pass/fail to "satisfaction." The agent's current verification is binary: did the tool call succeed? What it needs is: does the UI actually look different? The agent can't verify visual output. It can't see the UI. So it assumes that if echo "css content" > file.css succeeded, the theme is working. That's the fundamental limitation.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: That's an important point. The hardening layers were built around Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-1M's specific failure patterns — the tool arg malformation that the meta-reasoning gate catches, the attention decay that informed the personality persistence decision, the context pressure behaviors that BST and HTN compensate for. A different model will have different failure patterns. But here's what should transfer cleanly and what won't: Model-agnostic (works with any model): Organization kernel — role profiles, SALUTE reports, org hierarchy. These are pure scaffolding that never touch the model's reasoning. The dispatcher routes based on BST domain classification, not model-specific behavior. SALUTE emission and PACE monitoring — these read state from extension hooks, not from model output patterns. HTN plan templates — step sequences with verification gates. The model follows the plan context in its extras regardless of architecture. Supervisor loop — anomaly detection based on turn counts, failure counters, and context fill. Model-independent signals. Tool fallback chain — error classification uses regex on tool output, not model behavior. The advice injection works through hist_add_warning which any model sees.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Model-sensitive (may need tuning): BST trigger words and confidence thresholds — different models respond to different enrichment patterns. Qwen might need explicit slot context while another model might perform worse with it. Meta-reasoning gate — the specific arg aliases and value corrections were mapped from Qwen's observed mistakes. A different model might malform tool calls in different ways. Might send language: "python" instead of runtime: "bash". The alias maps would need expanding. Personality injection — attention decay is model-specific. A model with better long-range attention might hold Zero's voice deeper into context without the bookend compromise. Tiered tool injection — how much spec detail the model needs varies. A stronger model might work fine with just the compact menu. A weaker model might need full specs for every tool.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The interesting question is Qwen3 specifically. The architecture difference between Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 matters. If unsloth/qwen3-14b has better instruction following and tool use training, some of your hardening layers become less necessary — which is actually the goal. The meta-reasoning gate catches fewer malformed calls because the model makes fewer mistakes. The fallback advisor fires less often. The supervisor stays quiet longer. The scaffolding doesn't disappear, it just activates less frequently, acting as a safety net rather than a constant crutch. The way to test it cleanly: swap the model, don't change any hardening configuration, and run the same tasks. Watch the logs. If you see fewer [BST] enrichments needed, fewer meta-gate corrections, fewer fallback advisor activations, and the supervisor staying quieter — the new model is stronger within the same scaffolding. If you see new failure patterns the current layers don't catch, those become the next hardening targets. The organizational kernel is the part I'd be most confident survives a model swap untouched. It's the layer furthest from model-specific behavior. The meta-reasoning gate alias maps are the part most likely to need updates. Everything else falls on a spectrum between those two. Want to think about a model evaluation framework — a structured way to profile a new model's failure patterns against the hardening layers so you know what to tune?

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Good. Now I have the full picture of what exists. Let me think about what "Attractor integration" actually means at this stage — what's buildable tonight on top of what's deployed, and what's genuinely powerful versus architecturally elegant but premature. The three Attractor concepts we deferred: Graph-based workflows — replacing linear HTN step sequences with directed graphs that support branching, parallel paths, and conditional transitions Event-driven observability — typed event stream that the supervisor and future UIs consume in real-time Provider-aligned tool profiles — model-specific tool interfaces per role Number 3 is model tuning work — we just agreed to defer that. Number 2 is powerful but the supervisor loop already works with SALUTE snapshots and direct state reads. The real upgrade there comes with macrocosm when you need real-time cross-container awareness. Number 1 is the one that changes everything. Here's why:

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Right now HTN plans are linear: step 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. The bugfix workflow goes reproduce → isolate → fix → test → verify. But real debugging doesn't work that way. You reproduce, then either you can isolate immediately OR you need more information, so you branch to gather context, then come back to isolation. After fixing, if the test fails, you don't go to step 5 — you loop back to step 3. The linear plan can't express this. The agent either follows the sequence rigidly or ignores it entirely. A graph-based plan for the same workflow: reproduce → [success?] → yes: isolate → fix → test → [pass?] → yes: verify → done → no: loop back to fix (max 2) → no: gather_context → reproduce (max 2) → no after 2: escalate That's a fundamentally more expressive structure that matches how tasks actually flow. And it integrates directly with PACE — the "escalate" node is a PACE contingent trigger. The "max 2 retries" is the autonomous retry limit from the role doctrine.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Let me spec this: Created a file, ran a command, read a file The key design decision: this replaces the HTN plan selector, it doesn't sit alongside it. Same file, same hook point, same _15_ prefix. The graph engine is a strict superset — linear plans with steps arrays still work unchanged, but plans with a graph field get the full traversal engine with branching, retry loops, and escalation nodes. What makes this powerful versus the linear HTN: The bugfix workflow you watched earlier went straight through step 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 or stalled. The graph version has a reproduce → gather_context → reproduce loop for when reproduction fails, a fix → test → fix retry loop with bounded attempts, and an explicit escalation node that triggers PACE contingent when retries exhaust. The model doesn't decide to loop or escalate — the graph structure determines it based on verification outcomes. Deterministic routing, zero model reasoning.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The event log is the lightweight Attractor bridge. Every node transition, verification, retry, and escalation gets a typed event appended to the traversal state. The supervisor can now read not just "agent is on node X" but "agent went reproduce → isolate → fix → fix(retry) → fix(retry)" — that trajectory tells the supervisor the agent is struggling with the fix, which is much richer signal than a bare turn counter. All 10 existing plans get converted to graph format with meaningful branching. The spec includes 5 detailed graph structures and asks Claude Code to design the remaining 5 using the same patterns. Same Claude Code prompt pattern as before — point it at the spec, tell it to read the existing source, let it make implementation decisions. Attractor integration spec l3
