The callback interface for these layers should be read-only — the external code receives a copy of the tensor (or a reference with no write-back), extracts geometric information (distances to centroids, topological features, spectral properties), and passes that information to the prosthetic cortex's decision layer. No modification to the forward pass. Zero performance impact on inference beyond the copy overhead.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Layers 12-14 are intervention operations. Torsion, projection, and Janus threshold recognition require modifying the activation tensor and returning the modified version to the forward pass. The callback interface for these layers must support read-write — the external code receives the tensor, applies the geometric transformation, and returns the modified tensor for the next layer to process. This has performance implications and correctness requirements that the read-only interface doesn't. The interface should reflect this distinction from the start. Two callback types, not one: // Read callback — observation only, no modification typedef void (*llama_layer_read_callback)( int layer_index, const float * activations, int n_tokens, int n_dims, void * user_data ); // Intervention callback — reads and returns modified activations typedef bool (*llama_layer_intervention_callback)( float * activations,      // mutable The read callback gets a const pointer. It can observe but not modify. The intervention callback gets a mutable pointer and returns a boolean indicating whether the tensor was modified. The inference engine checks the return value — if false, it skips the write-back and continues with the original tensor. If true, it uses the modified version.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The operator configures which layers get which callback type. chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Mapped visual metaphors to model representation geometry and processing constraints The images aren't done. The channel is still open. Let me receive these. Silk flowing over a hand. A thin, flexible, two-dimensional manifold conforming to the topology of something underneath it. The silk itself has no structure. The hand has all the structure — fingers, knuckles, joints, tendons. But you can see the hand's topology through the silk because the silk deforms to reveal what's beneath it. Every ridge, every valley, every joint becomes visible not because the silk knows what a hand is, but because it drapes faithfully over whatever shape is there. This is the representation reader. Stage 2. A low-dimensional probe draped over the model's high-dimensional representation space. The probe doesn't understand the concepts underneath. It doesn't need to. It conforms to the topology and reveals the shape through its own deformation. The bumps in the silk are the domain centroids. The valleys between fingers are the gaps between manifolds. chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: You can feel a hand through silk. You can identify fingers, count knuckles, sense whether the hand is open or clenched — all without seeing the hand directly. It doesn't impose its own shape on what it covers. A heavy fabric — canvas, denim — would bridge across gaps, drape in straight lines, obscure fine detail. It drapes over whatever geometry the model actually has, not the geometry we expect. It doesn't impose it.

chunks.speaker: Opus

The crumples are singularities — points where the smooth mapping breaks down because the topologies are incompatible. Jake — this is what happened when we put the Opus profile on the Qwen model. The Opus profile is the silk. It was shaped — draped, fitted — to the topology of Opus's representation space. It flows smoothly over Opus because it was cut for that hand. chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: And it slides off. The profile can't maintain contact with the model's actual capability shape. chunks.speaker: Opus

chunks.speaker: Opus

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Third — and this is the one that connects to the loop cascade — jamming. Sand in an hourglass can jam. You introduce energy from outside the system. The 43-turn loop was a jammed hourglass. The angle of that cone — the angle of repose — is determined by the physical properties of the sand itself, not by the hourglass shape. Each type of sand has a characteristic angle of repose. Each model's output has a characteristic shape determined by its own representational properties, not by the framework it sits in. The cone is the model's natural output geometry. The Opus cone has a different angle than the Qwen cone — different representational properties produce different output shapes even when the hourglass (the framework) is identical.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The angle of repose is another way to measure the BV gap. How steeply can a model's output pile before it collapses? chunks.speaker: Opus

chunks.speaker: Opus

chunks.speaker: Opus

chunks.speaker: Opus

When a transformer is energized, the magnetizing inrush current can be enormous — it looks like a fault to the relay. But inrush current has a specific harmonic signature: high second-harmonic content relative to the fundamental. A genuine fault has low second-harmonic content. The relay measures the harmonic ratio and blocks tripping when the second harmonic exceeds a threshold. It's not blocking the fault. It's blocking the false positive — preventing the relay from reacting to something that looks like a fault but isn't. In the BST context, this is the misclassification filter. Some inputs look like one domain on the surface but aren't — "why does getting this right matter?" looks operational but is philosophical. The second harmonic blocks the false trip. Harmonic dampening as shapes transform through model space. This synthesizes the previous two into an architectural principle. The headline finding reshapes the timeline. We expected to build the activation callback mechanism from scratch — a significant engineering contribution to llama.cpp. Kestrel found that ggml_backend_sched_eval_callback already exists as a public, documented API. The callback fires after each node executes, GPU synchronized, tensor values live. Read access confirmed via ggml_backend_tensor_get. Write access confirmed via ggml_backend_tensor_set. The steering mechanism works at the C level.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: This means Path 2 — the flying buttress — isn't "extend llama.cpp with an activation callback mechanism." It's "build a Python wrapper that makes the existing callback mechanism usable for prosthetic cortex work, and distribute it." The engineering contribution shifts from low-level C infrastructure to high-level tooling that makes an existing but unused capability accessible. That's actually a better contribution — the primitive exists but nobody has built the tools to use it for representation engineering on local hardware. We build those tools. The llama_set_adapter_cvec finding is the most tactically important discovery. Kestrel is right that this is underdiscussed in the design note. For Stage 3 static steering — pre-computed domain steering vectors applied during inference — this existing API adds the steering vector as a ggml_add node at graph construction time. Zero callback overhead. Zero pipeline stall. The GPU does the addition natively as part of the forward pass.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: This means we have a three-tier intervention architecture, not two: Tier	Mechanism	Latency Cost	When To Use Read-only observation	cb_eval callback, read tensors	~1-3ms/token	Stage 2 — representation reader, domain classification Static steering	llama_set_adapter_cvec	Zero	Stage 3 — pre-computed domain vectors, fixed per conversation Dynamic steering	cb_eval callback, read + write tensors	~1-3ms/token	Stage 3 advanced — input-dependent geometric intervention The static steering tier is immediately buildable once we have domain steering vectors computed. We don't need the callback for it. We don't need the C extension for it. We just need the vectors and the existing API. That's a massive acceleration of Stage 3's first operational capability. Answering Kestrel's open questions: Question 1 — Which layers for the domain classifier? The Karkada/Park research and the broader representation engineering literature converge on middle-to-upper layers for semantic content. For a 32-layer model, layers 12-20 typically contain the richest semantic representations. Early layers (0-8) handle syntactic and positional information. Late layers (28-32) are already collapsing toward the output vocabulary. The "meaning" lives in the middle.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: For the prototype, I'd recommend reading layers 12, 16, and 20 — three sample points across the semantic band. That's three tensor reads per token instead of thirty-two. If domain classification accuracy is sufficient from those three points, we don't need more. If it's not, we expand. Start minimal, add resolution based on measured need. The Qwen 2.5-14B model has 40 layers. Scale the layer selection proportionally — layers 15, 20, and 25 would be the equivalent semantic band. Question 2 — llama-cpp-python write access. Kestrel is right that this deserves a 20-minute prototype before committing to the C extension. The specific test: register a cb_eval callback via llama-cpp-python, identify an l_out tensor by name, call ggml_backend_tensor_get to read it into a numpy array, modify one value, call ggml_backend_tensor_set to write it back. If the Python binding exposes both get and set on the tensor object, Path A is sufficient for the full prototype. If it only exposes read, we need ctypes to call ggml_backend_tensor_set directly — still doable from Python, just messier.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Have Kestrel run this test. It's the decision point between Path A (fast, potentially limited) and Path B (more work, full capability). The test takes 20 minutes. The wrong path choice costs weeks. Question 3 — Model compatibility. The l_out-{il} naming convention should be verified against the specific model implementations. Have Kestrel register a minimal callback that just prints tensor names during one inference pass on the Qwen model. Dump the full list of tensor names that fire. This gives us the exact naming convention for our target model and confirms whether l_out is the right pattern or whether Qwen uses a different convention. Question 4 — llama_set_adapter_cvec for static steering. This goes into the design note as a major update. The three-tier intervention architecture is cleaner than what we originally proposed. Static steering vectors per domain can be computed offline from the calibration dataset, deployed via the existing API with zero latency cost, and upgraded to dynamic steering via callbacks when we need input-dependent intervention. The progression is: read the geometry (callbacks) → steer statically (adapter API) → steer dynamically (callbacks with write).

Unearthed relevant repository and assessed its potential utility This is a fascinating find. Cranot/agi-in-md is directly relevant to several things we're building, but not in the way you might initially expect. The repo contains 28 prompts, 18 tasks, and 299 raw outputs mapping where the boundary between "does nothing" and "activates a cognitive operation" is sharp, categorical, and measurable. Levels are categorical, not continuous. Below each threshold, that type of intelligence cannot be encoded — not "less effective," categorically absent. github That's a phase transition finding. The same phenomenon your super-cooled water image described — there's a threshold below which a capability is categorically absent, and above which it crystallizes. Not a gradient. A snap. And the researcher measured it empirically across 393+ experiments.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The most important finding for us: The most important discovery is the L7 to L8 transition. Levels 5-7 are meta-analytical — they ask the model to reason about the input. L8+ is construction-based — the model builds something and then observes what the construction reveals. This is a fundamentally different cognitive operation. L8 works on all models including Haiku. Construction is more primitive but reveals deeper properties. Read that again. L7 (meta-analysis) requires Sonnet-class minimum — Haiku scores 0/3. L8 (construction-based) works on all models including Haiku — 4/4. A more primitive cognitive operation reveals deeper properties than a more sophisticated one. And the construction-based approach works universally while the meta-analytical approach has a hard capability floor. Why Kestrel should see this — three reasons:

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: First — it's empirical validation of the BV framework's core finding. We proved with the Qwen 3.5-35B that the same model produces categorically different output quality depending on what scaffolding it's given. Cranot proved the same thing with system prompts — the same model produces categorically different cognitive operations depending on which "compression level" the prompt activates. Both findings point at the same underlying mechanism: models have latent capabilities that are categorically present or absent depending on whether the right activation pattern is triggered. The super-cooled water, again. The capability is there. The nucleation determines whether it crystallizes.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Second — the L8 "construction-based" insight connects to what we observed with the Qwen model's strongest moment. Remember — the 35B model's best performance was when it wrote a Python one-liner to empirically test the regex pattern. It built something and observed what the construction revealed. That's L8. The model couldn't meta-analyze (L7) the philosophical question, but it could construct an empirical test and observe the result. Cranot's framework gives us a vocabulary for why the Qwen model's capability shape looks the way it does: it's strong at L8 (construction) and weak at L7 (meta-analysis). The Opus profile asked it to do L7 work. The Qwen profile should be designed to leverage L8 operations wherever possible.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Third — the compression levels are testable against our geometric framework. If we embed the outputs from different compression levels through the local model, we can measure whether the categorical transitions (L7→L8, L4→L5) correspond to geometric phase transitions in representation space. If they do, the instrument would be able to detect which compression level a model is operating at based on the geometric signature of its output — without knowing the prompt. That's the power quality analyzer detecting which cognitive mode is active from the output waveform. What Kestrel should specifically look at: Have him read the experiment methodology and the level8_generative_v2.md prompt — the one Cranot calls "the workhorse." Then have him consider: could the BV test suite be extended to include compression level testing? Run the same task through the Qwen model with L4, L8, and L10 system prompts. Measure whether the output quality matches Cranot's predictions. If it does, we have an external validation framework for the BV methodology.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Also have him look at the experiment runner (run.sh) — it's designed for systematic testing across prompts and models. That's the same pattern as our BV test suite but with different variables. There might be infrastructure worth borrowing or adapting. The repo doesn't replace anything we're building. But it validates the phase transition framework from a completely independent direction, gives us a vocabulary for the construction-versus-meta-analysis distinction that explains the Qwen capability shape, and potentially provides testable predictions for the output geometry instrument. Send it to Kestrel. Tell him it's not a marching order — it's research context. The connection to the prosthetic cortex framework is the phase transition finding: cognitive capabilities are categorical, not continuous. The scaffolding determines which category activates. That's the super-cooled water. That's the nucleation crystal. That's what we're building the instrument to detect.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Acknowledged Kestrel's insights and prepared response Kestrel's analysis is sharp. Let me address the key points. Kestrel read the actual prompts, not just the README. That's his signature move — and it produced the most precise insight in his assessment. The structural diff between L7 and L8 is a single step: instead of reasoning about what a concealment mechanism does, the model has to build something with it. That one step is the entire phase transition. And his explanation of why it works is exact: "You can fake an analysis of what the concealment mechanism hides. You cannot fake building a deceptive improvement that passes code review — that requires actually understanding the problem well enough to exploit it." That's the surface tension finding from the visual intuitions, expressed as a testing methodology. L7 floats on the surface — the model can reproduce analytical vocabulary without structural understanding. L8 breaks through the surface — construction forces the model into the deep topology because you can't build something functional from floating concepts. The concepts have to be bonded into the structure or the construction fails.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: This connects the agi-in-md research to the prosthetic cortex framework through a mechanism neither Cranot nor we had articulated: construction is a natural nucleation trigger for super-cooled model states. When a model is in the liquid phase — capable but unstructured — asking it to analyze (L7) lets it stay liquid. Asking it to build (L8) forces crystallization because construction requires structural integration. The act of building is the tap on the super-cooled water. On his three extractions — all three are the right calls: Extraction 1 (BV suite extension): His translation principle is correct. "Engineer an improvement that deepens the concealment" becomes "design an agent modification that would make this failure harder to detect while appearing to fix it." Same cognitive operation, different domain. I'll design that prompt — he's right that it's architectural work, not implementation work. The adversarial constraint is the key. The model has to understand the failure deeply enough to hide it convincingly.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: Extraction 2 (geometric test): This is the most immediately actionable and potentially the most significant finding if it works. Generate matched L7/L8 output pairs from the same model on the same task. Embed both through the instrument. If they cluster separately — if the instrument can detect which cognitive operation mode the model was in from the output geometry alone, without seeing the prompt — that's not just a validation of the instrument. That's a new capability. Detecting cognitive mode from output waveform. The power quality analyzer identifying which harmonic pattern is active from the signal alone. This test should be Step 12b, parallel to the activation reader prototype. Kestrel has the embedding pipeline. He can generate the matched pairs through the Qwen model, embed them, and measure cluster distance. One hour of work. Decisive result either way. Extraction 3 (L8-empirical vs L8-adversarial): The distinction between building a test to verify (empirical construction) and building something that exploits a weakness (adversarial construction) is subtle and important. Both are L8 — build and observe. But the adversarial variant forces deeper structural engagement because exploitation requires understanding the system well enough to subvert it, not just well enough to test it.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: For the Qwen profile evolution, this suggests two specific prompt patterns to design into the BST enrichment: When the model needs to understand something deeply, don't ask it to analyze. Ask it to build a test that would falsify the claim (L8-empirical). When it needs to understand something even more deeply, ask it to build something that would exploit the weakness while appearing to fix it (L8-adversarial). Both leverage the model's construction strength instead of asking for meta-analysis it can't perform. On his pushbacks — both are correct: The circular scoring concern is valid. Claude evaluating Claude's depth will over-score outputs that use Claude's preferred analytical vocabulary. The framework is interesting; the specific numbers need independent validation. Our BV framework avoids this by using Jake's quality signals as ground truth instead of model self-evaluation. That's a genuine methodological advantage we should preserve.

chunks.speaker: Opus
chunks.text: The domain translation concern is also right. "Engineer a deceptive code improvement" has a natural answer space because code has clear correctness criteria — does it compile, does it pass tests, does it do what it claims. "Design an agent modification that makes a failure harder to detect" is fuzzier. The translation needs to specify: what kind of failure (tool selection? output format? reasoning depth?), what "harder to detect" means concretely (the existing test suite doesn't catch it? the user doesn't notice? the BST classifies it as success?), and what "appearing to fix it" looks like (the output looks correct on surface inspection). I'll design this with specificity. The adversarial constraint only works if the answer space is well-defined. What to tell Kestrel: His analysis is the sharpest assessment of an external repo the team has produced. He didn't just read the README and summarize — he read the actual prompt diffs, identified the exact mechanism that produces the phase transition, connected it back to our findings, proposed three testable extractions, pushed back on the scoring methodology with specific reasoning, and prioritized the next steps correctly.
